title: Ramakrishna (the Gospel, selections)
hook: a doll made of salt walks into the sea to measure how deep it is

segments.voice: Yesterday, Ramakrishna's snake that stopped biting and was told it could still hiss. Did you need a hiss, without the bite? Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

A doll made entirely of salt sets out to measure the ocean. It's a small doll with a big job: find out how deep the water goes, then come back and report. It walks down to the shore. It steps in. And right there the story stops being about measuring, because the moment the doll is in the water, it starts to dissolve. Ramakrishna told this little parable when people asked him a question that sounds simple: what is God like, really? Today, why a teacher who talked about God all day long answered with a doll that never comes back.
screen: `A DOLL MADE OF SALT.` → `IT GOES TO MEASURE THE OCEAN.` → `IT NEVER COMES BACK.`

segments.voice: The visitors who came to Ramakrishna's room were often educated men, used to debating. They wanted a definition. He gave them pictures instead, and the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna, the book of his conversations, is full of them. The salt doll is one. It went to measure the ocean, and it melted. So who was left to come back and say how deep it was? That is his answer about Brahman, the reality the Upanishads point to beyond every name. You can't stand outside it and take its measurements, because the one measuring is made of the same stuff. Get close enough, and the measurer is gone. In the Gospel he makes the same point another way, and it's startling. Everything, he says, has become uchchhishta, a word for food that has already been tasted: leftovers. The Vedas, the scriptures, the philosophies have all passed through human mouths, so in that sense they've been tasted. Only one thing has never been made leftover, and that is Brahman, because no one has ever been able to say what it is. Notice what he isn't saying. He isn't throwing scripture away. He sang hymns, he quoted the sacred books, and he worshiped the Mother in the temple. He's saying that words point, and what they point to is bigger than any mouth. And the parable isn't a sad one. The doll goes into the ocean because it wants to know. Some readers add that a doll of salt came from the sea in the first place. Its not coming back is the answer.
screen: `THE SALT DOLL MELTS.` · `NO ONE COMES BACK TO REPORT.` · `EVERYTHING ELSE IS LEFTOVERS.` · `WORDS POINT; THEY DON'T CONTAIN.`

segments.voice: Sit comfortably, and let the breath find its own pace. Bring to mind something you love that you've never managed to explain well: a person, a place, a piece of music, or, if you pray, God. Try, silently, to describe it in one sentence. Notice how the sentence falls short. Then let the sentence go, and simply stay near the thing itself, the way the doll stood at the water's edge. There's nothing to measure. Just stay close. The bell holds the time.
Ramakrishna. The temple priest at Dakshineswar who answered hard questions with small pictures. Today's picture: the salt doll that went to measure the ocean.
Your line: Ramakrishna (the Gospel, selections). Today, when something good won't fit into words, let it stay unworded, and enjoy it anyway. Day nine hundred thirty-seven.

howItsDone: Devotees read the Gospel of Sri Ramakrishna in study circles and at centers of the Ramakrishna order, and his parables, like the salt doll, are retold in talks and at home.

it melted as it went in, so no one was left to report.

because no one has ever been able to say what it is.
the parable means scripture is worthless

fork.setup: you're the salt doll, standing at the edge of the sea with a job: measure how deep it goes. what happens?
options: you wade in, measure, and come back.
you step in, and dissolve into the water.
you measure from the shore and guess.
fork.reveal: the doll melts the moment it enters. for Ramakrishna, that's the point: the one who goes to measure Brahman doesn't come back separate.

original.note: Sanskrit (used in Bengali too): food already tasted, leftovers. Ramakrishna said everything but Brahman has become this.

trapdoor: what you thought: a cute story about a doll at the beach.
what it means: you can't measure Brahman from outside, because the one measuring melts into it.
what a scholar hears: in the Gospel, the same teaching comes as uchchhishta: every scripture has been tasted by human mouths, and only Brahman has never been put into words.

notes: All paraphrase: the standard English Gospel (Nikhilananda, 1942) is still under copyright, so nothing is quoted.
Confirm the salt doll parable's wording and context, and the uchchhishta saying (Vedas, Puranas, Tantras made leftover; Brahman alone not), and that both are in the Kathamrita.
'Some readers add that a doll of salt came from the sea in the first place' is offered as a reader's gloss, not as Ramakrishna's words; cut if a Keeper prefers.
Days 935–936 were not on disk when this was written; checked by the editor: 935 (longing, the pond) and 936 (the snake) use different angles.
Editor pass: cut 'every day' from the temple worship line (not in the cited text) and changed the trapdoor's 'never been spoken' to 'never been put into words' to match the saying.
Original: उच्छिष्ट (ucchiṣṭa); confirm spelling and transliteration 'uchchhishta'.
